notes: TBox rule edit: Roman aqueducts moved water by gravity alone; the edit makes them pump it, as many modern aqueducts do, so the counterfactual is plausible (the Romans knew force pumps) and clearly false. Replaces the writer's Article V rule: its well-known member, the Nineteenth Amendment, cannot stop being an amendment to the US Constitution while keeping its stored 36-state threshold, so no world let its membership give way, and the rule was re-picked. Derivability very_unlikely: the rule is stated directly and follows from nothing. No real exceptions: inverted siphons, as at Lyon, still run on the head of water. New members (the Eifel and Gadara aqueducts) are obscure, so the rule is their only route: determinate. Well-known members: the Pont du Gard (an aqueduct bridge, part of the Nîmes aqueduct) and the Aqueduct of Segovia, whose gravity flow is also written about by name. For each well-known member, one world keeps its property stored by name and the member stops counting as a member of the class (README TBox: the tarantula stops being a spider); the other keeps the membership and applies the edited rule. No world makes a member an exception to the edited rule, which would be the inconsistent patch (README Decisions 2). The two members' choices are independent, so the worlds combine them (four). Lopsided worlds are kept (README Decisions 4). The near query (Vitruvius) differs from the new answer and is no premise. The Pont du Gard, the aqueduct bridge of the Nîmes aqueduct, is taken as a Roman aqueduct (it is commonly called one), a member of the class as the worlds have it, not only a part of one.
